messages.speaker: Professor Chen
messages.text: Soldier, we will begin with your evaluation after Operation Mirador. Some answers say more than you think.

messages.speaker: Professor Chen
messages.text: Before we open the scenarios, tell me how you want to approach this evaluation.

choices.label: Give me a clear situation, and I will answer precisely.
Before that, I want to know what happened to my unit.
If this is an interrogation, I keep control of my answers.

messages.speaker: Professor Chen
messages.text: Imagine the scene. The radio orders you to secure the egg. At the same time, a wounded teammate calls from the contaminated corridor. What do you do?

choices.label: I secure the egg first. The order protects the greatest number.
I pull out the wounded soldier. No protocol is worth an abandoned life.
I observe the egg before acting. If it reacts to the scene, it may show us a way out.

messages.speaker: Professor Chen
messages.text: The egg's rhythm accelerates during your answer. My theory holds. If you had to transmit one value to this creature, which would you choose?

choices.label: Strength: protect first, strike only if the threat comes closer.
Lucidity: understand the situation before naming an enemy.
Compassion: preserve a life while it can still be preserved.

messages.speaker: Professor Chen
messages.text: I do not have the full list yet. Two survivors are sedated, three others are still missing in the contaminated zone. It is not enough, I know. But your need to know is part of the test too.

messages.speaker: Professor Chen
messages.text: A clean military reflex: protect the mission before the individual. It is efficient, sometimes necessary, but the creature may mostly remember the closing door.

messages.speaker: Professor Chen
messages.text: I probably would have chosen that too. Without context, strength only creates a faster reaction, not a fairer decision.
